# Unity Package Manager packages

## Detect
- A UPM package folder has a `package.json` whose `name` is reverse-domain (for example `com.example.tool`), next to some of `Runtime/`, `Editor/`, `Tests/`, `Samples~/` or `Samples/`, `Documentation~/` or `Documentation/`, and `CHANGELOG.md`. A `package.json` without that `name` shape belongs to another stack (for example Node); ignore this pack there.
- Mutability: an embedded package (`Packages/<name>/`) and a local folder referenced as `"<name>": "file:<path>"` in a project's `Packages/manifest.json` (relative paths start from `Packages/`) can be changed; registry, Git URL, and tarball installs are read-only.
- Packages outside `Assets/` and `Packages/` (for example at the repository root): their C# files match neither pack's default globs. Bind the package folder (for example `com.example.tool/**`) to both `unity` and `unity-upm` with `stack_paths` in the profile, keeping each pack's default globs the project still needs in its list (see `[stack_paths]` in the [profile template](.ai/kit/core/templates/project/profile.toml)), and activate both.
- Host project: Unity compiles and tests a package only inside a project. Find it through `commands.build`/`commands.test` or a `Packages/manifest.json` that references the package with `file:` and lists it in `testables`.
- Samples convention: the folder name (`Samples~` or `Samples`), the prefix of each `samples[].path`, and any `.sample.json` files under the samples folder (see «Version Notes»).
- Release tags: `git tag --list` shows whether releases are tagged per package or per repository.

## Conventions
- `package.json`: `name` (required) uses reverse-domain notation with only lowercase letters, digits, `-`, `_`, and `.`, within 50 characters (the hard limit is 214); never start it with `com.unity` or put `unity` anywhere in it. `version` (required) is SemVer `major.minor.patch`. Set `unity` to the lowest supported Editor as `major.minor` (`"6000.0"` for Unity 6; optional `unityRelease` such as `"0b4"`), plus `displayName` and `description`. Optional fields, when present, must hold valid values.
- `dependencies` maps package names to exact SemVer versions: no ranges, and no Git URLs (those are allowed only in a project's `Packages/manifest.json`).
- Licensing: `license` holds an SPDX identifier or a pointer to `LICENSE.md`; omit it only when the package root has a `LICENSE.md`. Notices for bundled third-party code or DLLs go in `Third Party Notices.md` at the package root.
- One asmdef per code folder: `Runtime/<org>.<package>.asmdef`, `Editor/<org>.<package>.Editor.asmdef` (Editor platform only, references Runtime), `Tests/Runtime/<org>.<package>.Tests.asmdef`, `Tests/Editor/<org>.<package>.Editor.Tests.asmdef`. The Editor ignores package scripts outside an asmdef; Runtime never references Editor.
- Optional dependency on another package: leave it out of `dependencies`. In the asmdef that uses it, add a `versionDefines` entry `{ "name": "<package>", "expression": "<version or range>", "define": "<SYMBOL>" }`, then guard the code with `#if <SYMBOL>`, or move it to its own asmdef that references the package and lists `<SYMBOL>` in `defineConstraints`, so it compiles only when the package is installed. The symbol is visible only inside that assembly.
- `versionDefines` expressions: `[1.3,3.4.1]` inclusive, `(1.3.0,3.4)` exclusive, `[2.4.5]` exact, a bare `2.1.0` means that version or later; no spaces or wildcards.
- `samples`: one entry per sample subfolder with `displayName`, `path`, and optional `description` and `images` (see «Version Notes»); keep the path prefix the package already uses. Keep sample metadata in either the `samples` array or one `.sample.json` per folder directly under the samples folder, never both: a single `.sample.json` makes packing ignore the whole array, and a sample without its own `.sample.json` is then missing from the installed package.
- Keep a `CHANGELOG.md` at each package root and add an entry with every `version` bump.
- A repository holding several packages: version each package independently and tag each release with the package name and version (for example `com.example.tool-v1.2.0`), so a consumer can pin `<repo>.git?path=/<folder>#<tag>`; one repository-wide tag cannot pin packages separately.

## Verify
- Prefer `commands.build` and `commands.test`; otherwise run the `unity` pack's batch compile and test commands on the host project.
- Package tests run in a host project only when the package is embedded or listed in that project's `testables` (for example `"testables": ["com.example.tool"]` in `Packages/manifest.json`).
- `package.json` parses as JSON, and its `version` matches the newest `CHANGELOG.md` entry.
- `git ls-files <package folder>` lists a `.meta` beside every file and folder outside `~` folders.
- After changing `samples`, import each changed sample into the host project from the Package Manager window and check the console for errors.

## Pitfalls
- Unity skips files and folders whose names end in `~` or start with `.` during import, so `Samples~/` and `Documentation~/` get no Unity-generated `.meta`, no compilation, and no Editor API access. Edit a sample through the host project's imported copy under `Assets/` or a link that exposes it, then copy the result back with the same file set the sample already tracks. With neither, editing its scenes or prefabs falls under the direct-YAML exception in the `unity` pack.
- Editing only the imported copy of a sample: it is a copy, not the package; the change stays in the host project until copied back.
- Missing `.meta` files in the package: GUID references need them, and registry and Git installs are read-only for consumers. Commit each package asset's `.meta` with the asset.
- Git URL order: `?path=` precedes `#revision` (`https://example.com/repo.git?path=/com.example.tool#com.example.tool-v1.2.0`); the reverse order fails. A revision is a branch, a tag, or a full commit hash; short hashes are unsupported. The project's lock file pins the resolved commit, so a branch URL stays on that commit until the dependency is requested again.
- Git LFS: without the LFS client, the Package Manager checks out LFS pointer files and reports no error, and because it clones shallowly, pointer files can arrive even with the client. Check that LFS-tracked files in an installed Git package hold content, not pointer text starting `version https://git-lfs`. A repository `.lfsconfig` (the LFS server URL) belongs in `.npmignore` so releases leave it out.
- Wildcards in a project's `scopedRegistries` `scopes` (`com.example.*`) do not work: list exact package names or a namespace prefix such as `com.example`. The closest match picks the registry, and a name no scope matches comes from the default registry.

## Version Notes
- Samples folder: the Unity 6.3 and 6.6 manuals have authors create `Samples/` with `samples[].path` starting `Samples`, and a Unity process that packs the package (for example Export) renames the folder to `Samples~`; the 6.6 manual adds that packing also fixes the paths in the copy consumers install, so leave them starting `Samples`. The Unity 6.0 manual has authors create `Samples~/` directly, with `Samples~/<name>` paths, and the current manifest reference still shows `Samples~/` paths. Keep the convention the package already uses unless asked to migrate (as of 2026-10, per Unity Manual 6000.0, 6000.3, and 6000.6 "Create samples for your package" and the package manifest reference).
- Create package (Unity 6.3 and 6.6 manuals) also writes `Samples/Example/.sample.json`, so packing ignores the `samples` array of a package it created until every `.sample.json` is deleted. A `.sample.json` holds `displayName`, `description`, and (6.6 manual) `images`, never `path`, because its folder sets the path; its `images` entries start with `Samples~/` even while the folder is `Samples` (as of 2026-10, per Unity Manual 6000.3 and 6000.6 "Create samples for your package").
- `samples[].images` first appears in the Unity 6.5 manual: optional image paths from the package root, starting with the sample's `path`, shown in the Package Manager's All Samples view (as of 2026-10, per Unity Manual 6000.5 and 6000.6 "Create samples for your package").
- Create package names `Samples` and `Documentation` without the tilde, while registry packages hide them with it; Export adds the tilde only to `Samples`. Before Export or sharing, rename `Documentation` to `Documentation~` in the Project window, not on disk, or ask the user to (as of 2026-10, per the Unity Manual package layout and "Document your package").
- Unity 6 values of `unity` use the `6000.x` form, for example `"6000.0"` (as of 2026-10, per the Unity Manual package manifest reference).
- Git dependencies need a Git client 2.14.0 or later on `PATH`, plus the Git LFS client for repositories that use LFS (as of 2026-10, per Unity Manual "Introduction to Git dependencies").
- Package signatures: from Unity 6.3 the Package Manager checks the signature of packages installed from a registry, a tarball, by name, or from the Asset Store, and flags unsigned or invalid ones; 6.3 builds before 6000.3.5f2 can flag a valid signature as invalid. A signed `.tgz` comes from the Package Manager window's export, batch mode `-upmPack <package folder> <output .tgz> -cloudOrganization <org id>`, the scripting API, or `upm pack` from the UPM CLI, a standalone tool that needs no Editor and signs with service account credentials. Every method signs for a Unity organization with its credentials, so leave signing to the user or CI (as of 2026-10, per the Unity Manual package signature and signing method pages, and its 6000.3 edition for the known issue).
- Unity 6.5 provides `System.Text.Json`, `System.Collections.Immutable`, `System.Reflection.Metadata`, and `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe` itself: a copy of these assemblies inside a package is dropped from the build whatever its version, and the package's code runs against Unity's version (as of 2026-10, per the Unity 6.5 upgrade guide).
- Unity 6.6 turns more packages into core packages that ship with the Editor, among them Cinemachine, Timeline, Animation Rigging, and Performance Testing (`com.unity.test-framework.performance`). A dependency on one resolves to the Editor's version, and Cinemachine 2 becomes Cinemachine 3, a different API. Check the core package list before depending on a Unity package (as of 2026-10, per the Unity 6.6 upgrade guide, What's New in Unity 6.6, and the core packages list).
- Unity Mathematics (6.5) and Burst (6.6) are built-in modules: their `Unity.Mathematics` and `Unity.Burst` APIs work with no package installed, yet neither appears in the core or built-in package lists. The manuals do not say how an existing `dependencies` entry or asmdef reference to them resolves, so confirm it by compiling the package in a host project on those versions (as of 2026-10, per What's New in Unity 6.5 and 6.6 and the core and built-in package lists).
- Unity 6.6 deprecates the `UNITY_64` and `DEVELOPMENT_BUILD` defines (analyzer warnings `UAC0008` and `UAC0009`, build errors under warnings-as-errors; the guide plans their removal for 6.8, after which using them is a compile error). The Unity 7.0 alpha (`7000.0.0a12`) already defines neither: there, `#if UNITY_64` and `#if DEVELOPMENT_BUILD` blocks compile out and their `#else` or `#if !` counterparts always compile, and its release notes do not say whether using the symbols warns or errors. Checks and assertions move to `UNITY_ENABLE_CHECKS` and profiling or diagnostic logging to `UNITY_INCLUDE_INSTRUMENTATION`, both set by the Managed Code Variant; `UNITY_64` becomes a runtime `IntPtr.Size == 8` check. Code that must not run in release Players, such as logging that could expose tokens, checks `Debug.isDebugBuild` at runtime instead, because a release Player can use the Checked variant. Code that also compiles on older Editors branches on `UNITY_6000_6_OR_NEWER`: the new defines from 6.6, `Debug.isDebugBuild` before it, and the `[Conditional]` symbol picked the same way (as of 2026-10, per the Unity 6.6 upgrade guide and the Unity `7000.0.0a12` release notes).
